title: ReNU SYNDROME
alt_titles: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, BRAIN ANOMALIES, DISTINCTIVE FACIES, AND ABSENT LANGUAGE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ReNU syndrome (RENU) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RNU4-2 gene, which encodes the U4 small nuclear RNA (snRNA) of the major spliceosome, on chromosome 12.

checks.claim: ReNU syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RNU4-2 gene.

paragraphs.text: ReNU syndrome is a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability, absent or very limited speech, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, and seizures (Greene et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Most affected individuals show brain MRI abnormalities and dysmorphic facial features, and involvement of other organ systems, including visual, gastrointestinal, and skeletal, is frequent (Chen et al., 2024). The disorder is caused by de novo variants in a short, highly constrained central region of RNU4-2, and Chen et al. (2024) estimated that variants in this region explain about 0.4% of individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) analyzed Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms recorded for 46 participants in the UK 100,000 Genomes Project (100KGP) who were coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality and carried RNU4-2 variants. Of these 46 cases, 91% had intellectual disability, 91% had neurodevelopmental delay, and 61% had motor delay. Terms significantly overrepresented compared with other neurodevelopmentally affected participants included microcephaly in 57% (vs 18%), drooling in 13% (vs 1%), proportionate short stature in 28% (vs 7%), generalized hypotonia in 39% (vs 13%), seizure in 52% (vs 27%), and abnormality of the upper lip vermilion in 13% (vs 2%). No terms were significantly underrepresented.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) collected detailed phenotypic information on 49 individuals (21 females and 28 males; median age at last evaluation 10 years, range 2 to 38 years) with RNU4-2 variants. All had global developmental delay (severe in 34 and moderate in 10) and all 45 assessed had intellectual disability. Of individuals older than 5 years, 83% were ambulatory, but walking was delayed (average 3.4 years, range 17 months to 7.5 years), with some having a wide-based or ataxic gait. Only 3 individuals had fluent speech; 35 of 45 with speech abnormality were nonverbal and 10 had a few words. Other features included short stature (76%), microcephaly (77%, mostly congenital), hypotonia (87%), seizures (77%), intrauterine growth restriction (18%), behavioral issues (67%), autism spectrum disorder (48%), sleep issues (47%), hearing loss (22%), and vision issues (79%), including optic nerve hypoplasia, strabismus, nystagmus, and cortical blindness. Seizure onset ranged from the first year of life to 10 years (median 3 years) and seizure types included infantile spasms, focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, febrile seizures, and status epilepticus. Brain MRI was abnormal in 91%, most frequently showing reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, and delayed myelination. Gastrointestinal problems included constipation, gastroesophageal reflux, and feeding difficulties, with 13 of 41 requiring a gastrostomy tube; skeletal abnormalities included osteopenia, recurrent fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, and hip dysplasia; and endocrine involvement included hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, and pituitary abnormalities. All but 3 individuals had dysmorphic facial features, which varied but included a myopathic face, deep-set eyes (some widely and some narrowly spaced), epicanthus, wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares or underdeveloped alae nasi, large cupped ears, full cheeks, a distinctive mouth with full lips and downturned corners, high-arched palate, and a large or protruding tongue. No significant differences between males and females were noted.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of ReNU syndrome is autosomal dominant; most cases result from de novo heterozygous variants (Greene et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Chen et al. (2024) found that in all 54 individuals in whom the parental origin could be confidently determined, the variant was on the maternal allele. Greene et al. (2024) observed one case that inherited the n.76C-T variant from an affected mother.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) compared the burden of rare variants in 41,132 noncoding genes between 5,529 unrelated cases with intellectual disability and 46,401 unrelated controls in the 100KGP using whole-genome sequencing data, and identified a strong dominant association with rare variants in RNU4-2. Variants clustered in 2 contiguous regions (n.62-70 and n.73-79) in which no unaffected participant carried a rare variant; these regions map to a quasi-pseudoknot interaction between U4 and U6 and to U4/U6 stem III. Of 47 rare alleles in these regions, found in 47 cases, 37 were de novo and 10 had unknown inheritance. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, occurred de novo in 33 families. In replication in 3 further UK collections, they identified 27 additional probands with a rare variant in the 2 regions, of whom 26 were affected; 19 of the 26 had a de novo variant, 6 had unknown inheritance, and 1 inherited n.76C-T from an affected mother, bringing the number of unrelated cases to 73. One parent was found to be mosaic for n.65A-G. The n.76C-T variant was the only variant present in gnomAD (1 allele in 152,108), and an n.76C-G variant was observed in 1 participant without neurodevelopmental abnormality, suggesting to the authors that some changes at position 76 may have milder or benign effects.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) identified a recurrent single-base insertion in RNU4-2, n.64_65insT, that occurred de novo in 38 probands with undiagnosed neurodevelopmental disorders in the Genomics England 100,000 Genomes Project; 8 more individuals without data for both parents also had the variant, giving 46 (0.52% of 8,841 undiagnosed probands). The variant was not found in 3,408 probands with a known genetic diagnosis, 21,817 probands with other phenotypes, or 33,122 unaffected individuals, and was absent from gnomAD v4.0 and All of Us. They defined an 18-bp critical region (nucleotides 62-79) depleted of variation in the population and, including additional cohorts, identified heterozygous variants in this region in 115 individuals; de novo occurrence was confirmed in 86 with sequencing data from both parents. Most (89; 77.4%) had n.64_65insT; the second recurrent insertion, n.77_78insT, was found in 6 individuals, including 2 affected sibs; and 15 individuals had single-nucleotide variants (10 confirmed de novo). In 1 individual, the n.65A-G variant appeared to be mosaic in the mother, and in another, the n.76C-T variant was maternally inherited.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) performed RNA sequencing on blood from 5 individuals with RNU4-2 variants (3 with n.64_65insT, 1 with n.77_78insT, and 1 with n.78A-C) and found increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites compared with controls (mean 8.8 vs 0.7 events). The unannotated 5-prime splice sites with increased use showed an increase in T at position +3 and C at positions +4 and +5, the positions that pair with the U6 ACAGAGA sequence. Twelve abnormal splicing events were shared by 2 or more affected individuals, none of which was found in 378 controls. Chen et al. (2024) also showed that RNU4-2 is expressed at a consistently higher level than its paralog RNU4-1 in human prefrontal cortex across development, and that chromatin around RNU4-2 is more accessible in prenatal cortex.

agent.process_note: I read all three papers in full: Greene et al. (2024) and Chen et al. (2024) as full texts, and Schot et al. (2024), which is available only as an abstract. I used Grep to check variant names (n.64_65insT, n.65A>G, n.76C>T, n.77_78insT, n.78A>C) and the case counts. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so the intro has no gene MIM number; the gene location is given only as chromosome 12, as stated by Chen et al. The name 'ReNU' and the alternative title do not appear in the papers, so I wrote no nomenclature section. I did not report variants that appear only in figure legends (n.63T>G, n.64_65insG, n.65_66insT, n.67A>G, n.68_69insA) as separate allelic variants. I wrote no animal-model section because none of the papers includes animal data.
